evidence: Ov. Met. 4.340: flexum genū (Lewis & Short s.v. flectō)
Sen. Herc. F. 410: inflexō genū adōrāre (Lewis & Short s.v. genū)
terms.comment: To bend the knee; kneeling is flexīs genibus, the school dialogues’ phrase for kneeling to pray (Corderius, Erasmus); Ovid and Seneca have the singular. The Orthodox churches keep the rule of the Council of Nicaea (canon 20) that on Sundays and from Easter to Pentecost prayer is made standing, until the kneeling prayers of Pentecost evening; in the Latin rite kneeling is a regular posture at Mass.
Curtius’s phrase (genū pōnere), and the Vulgate’s: positīs genibus ōrābat, he knelt down and prayed.

terms.gloss: go down on one’s knees (outside church too)
terms.comment: To sink onto one’s knees, of anyone kneeling down.

phrases.latin: flectō genua mea ad Patrem Dominī nostrī Jēsū Chrīstī
phrases.english: I bend my knees before the Father of our Lord Jesus Christ

phrases.latin: Flexīs genibus, et conjūnctīs manibus dīxī precātiōnem Dominicam, cum grātiārum āctiōne.
phrases.english: On my knees, with my hands together, I said the Lord’s Prayer and a thank-you.

phrases.latin: elephantum minimus Aethiops jubet subsīdere in genua et ambulāre per fūnem
phrases.english: the smallest African boy makes the elephant kneel down and walk the tightrope
